title: Clocks you can't trust: wall clocks, monotonic clocks and NTP
goal: By the end you can pick the right JVM clock for a duration and for a timestamp, estimate how far a synced clock can be off, show how last write wins drops acknowledged writes when two clocks disagree, and explain how a clock that reports its own error lets Spanner order writes with commit wait.

warmup.q: Pod B's clock is 15 ms behind pod A's. Pod A writes `captured` to a payment's status in Cassandra. 6 ms later pod B reads `captured` and writes `refunded`. Both get OK, and both use the driver's default client-side timestamps. What does the next read return?
options: `refunded`, because it was written last
`captured`, because B's write carries the older timestamp and is dropped
An error, because Cassandra detects the conflicting writes
Either one, at random
warmup.why: Cassandra keeps the write with the highest timestamp, and the timestamp comes from the writer's clock. B wrote 6 ms later in real time, but its clock is 15 ms behind, so its stamp is 9 ms older than A's. The replica drops it and still says OK. No error, no conflict: the order of the clocks beat the order of the events.

sections.body:
A JVM gives you two clocks, and they answer different questions. `System.currentTimeMillis()` answers "what time is it?": milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, the number you put in a log line or a `created_at` column. `System.nanoTime()` answers "how long did that take?": nanoseconds counted from an arbitrary starting point, which the JDK 25 documentation says may only be used to measure elapsed time. On Linux both are read through `clock_gettime` in the vDSO, without a real system call (the Operating systems track's first lesson): `currentTimeMillis` reads `CLOCK_REALTIME` and `nanoTime` reads `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`.

The **time-of-day clock**, or wall clock, tries to match real time, so it gets corrected, and a correction can be a jump. If NTP finds the clock 300 ms fast, it may step it back 300 ms; an operator can set it by hand. When a leap second is inserted (the last one was at the end of 2016), the day ends with 23:59:60, and the Linux kernel does that by stepping its clock back one second at midnight. Subtract two wall-clock readings across a step and the duration is wrong, perhaps negative.

That is what took down part of Cloudflare's DNS on 1 January 2017. Its DNS server, written in Go, timed round trips to upstream servers with `time.Now()`. When the leap second stepped the clock back, a round trip came out negative, the smoothed average went negative, and the code passed it to `rand.Int63n()`, which panics on a negative argument. At the peak about 0.2% of DNS queries failed. Go 1.9 later made `time.Time` carry a monotonic reading, so subtracting two times uses it.

The **monotonic clock** never jumps. NTP may still slew it, making it tick slightly faster or slower to correct its rate, but it never moves backward. Its value alone means nothing: it may count from boot, and another machine or another JVM counts from somewhere else, so comparing `nanoTime()` values across machines is meaningless.

The rule follows. Durations, timeouts and deadlines use `nanoTime()` or Kotlin's `TimeSource.Monotonic`. Points in time that must mean the same thing on another machine use the wall clock, and then you must assume it can be wrong; the rest of this lesson is about how wrong. Linux has two more clocks you'll meet: `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` is monotonic but keeps counting while the machine sleeps, and `CLOCK_TAI` is like `CLOCK_REALTIME` but counts leap seconds instead of repeating one. The Try replays Cloudflare's bug in Kotlin.

try.title: Your clocks, and a duration that goes negative
steps: Predict: what is the smallest step of `System.currentTimeMillis()` and of `System.nanoTime()` on your laptop?

Run the demo. Part 1 measures both. Part 2 times a 12 ms round trip twice, once with a wall clock that is stepped back one second in the middle (as a leap second or an NTP step would), once with `nanoTime`, and passes each result to `Random.nextLong(bound)`, which needs a positive bound, as Go's `rand.Int63n` did.
Open `WallClockDemo.kt` and find the one line that would have avoided the outage.
try.expect:
```text
currentTimeMillis: smallest step 1 ms (over 50 changes)
nanoTime:          smallest step 41 ns (over a million reads)
nanoTime now:      279138216654000 (an arbitrary origin: compare it only with this JVM's own readings)

round trip from the wall clock: -982 ms
round trip from nanoTime:       18 ms
Random.nextLong(-982) with the wall clock value: IllegalArgumentException: Random range is empty: [0, -982).
Random.nextLong(18) with the nanoTime value: 4
```

This run was on an Apple Silicon Mac, where `nanoTime` moves in steps of about 41 ns (a 24 MHz counter); on Linux in the lab box you will usually see much smaller steps, and the `nanoTime now` value is different on every machine. The round trips vary by a few milliseconds from run to run. The wall-clock round trip is the real 18 ms minus the 1,000 ms step, and the random call throws, as Go's did. `nanoTime` doesn't see the step at all.

sections.h: Quartz drifts, NTP pulls it back, and only a bound is honest
sections.body:
A computer's clock is a quartz crystal that vibrates at a nominal frequency, plus a counter. Real crystals run slightly fast or slow, depending on how they were cut and on temperature. The error is measured in parts per million (ppm): 1 ppm is 1 microsecond per second, about 86 ms a day. Google's Spanner paper assumes a worst case of 200 ppm, which is 17.28 seconds a day for a clock nobody corrects. Two servers drifting in opposite directions move apart even faster. The lab's `DriftDemo` runs one oscillator 150 ppm fast and one 120 ppm slow:

```text
sync                    fast clock, max  slow clock, max   max skew between
never                          12960 ms        -10368 ms           23328 ms
every hour                       539 ms          -431 ms             970 ms
every 64 s                         9 ms            -7 ms              16 ms
every 30 s                         4 ms            -3 ms               7 ms
```

NTP corrects the drift. The client asks a server for the time and keeps four timestamps: when it sent, when the server received, when the server replied, when the answer arrived. From them it estimates its offset, assuming the trip there took as long as the trip back. When it didn't (a queue in one direction, lesson 1), the estimate is off by up to half the difference, and NTP can't tell. So NTP's accuracy is limited by the network: over the public internet, tens of milliseconds is typical. chrony, the NTP client on RHEL and many other distributions, corrects small offsets by slewing and steps the clock only for large ones (`makestep 1 3`: step if off by more than a second in the first three updates).

Better sources shrink the error. Network cards that timestamp packets in hardware take the kernel's own queues out of the measurement; chrony's documentation says that with them, good switches and frequent polling, sub-microsecond accuracy on a LAN may be possible. PTP, the Precision Time Protocol, is built around such hardware timestamps. In November 2023 AWS brought this to EC2: its Time Sync Service reports a clock error bound under 100 µs over NTP and under 40 µs from a PTP hardware clock on Nitro instances, against about 1 ms before. AWS's open-source ClockBound daemon publishes that bound, so a program can read an interval, earliest to latest, instead of one number. The figure shows the bound's shape between syncs.

The bound can still be wrong. A Google Compute Engine VM that is live-migrated can see its clock jump forward by up to 5 seconds. A server whose NTP traffic is blocked by a firewall drifts and nobody notices. Leap seconds have caused outages (Reddit's Cassandra cluster in 2012), which is why Google and AWS smear them, slowing their clocks over a day instead of inserting the second; mixing smeared and unsmeared sources makes two clocks disagree by up to half a second. Leap seconds are on their way out: in October 2026 the CGPM, the treaty body behind the SI units, reportedly voted to stop inserting them from 20 May 2027. That rests on news reports and secondary summaries; the course hasn't seen the BIPM's own text, and the second edition of *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* still says 2035.

One more fact shapes how you test all this. Containers on one host share the kernel's wall clock: Linux time namespaces can offset the monotonic and boot clocks, never `CLOCK_REALTIME`. The Try proves it. To give one service a skewed clock, you hand its code a different `java.time.Clock`, which is what the lab does.

try.title: Containers share one wall clock
steps: Start Docker. From the `labs` folder, run the commands below. The first two start two different containers and print the kernel's boot id.
The third tries to set the wall clock inside an ordinary container. Predict whether it works.

The fourth runs in the privileged box: it prints the uptime (which comes from `CLOCK_BOOTTIME`) and the wall clock, then does the same inside a new time namespace whose boot and monotonic clocks are moved forward one day. Which number moves?

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box-priv cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box date -s '2026-01-01'
docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box-priv bash -c 'cut -d" " -f1 /proc/uptime; date -u +%T; unshare -T --boottime=86400 --monotonic=86400 bash -c "cut -d\" \" -f1 /proc/uptime; date -u +%T"'

try.expect:
```text
1f57facb-e375-427f-9481-750da423d763
1f57facb-e375-427f-9481-750da423d763
Thu Jan  1 12:00:00 AM UTC 2026
date: cannot set date: Operation not permitted
2896.76
06:26:47
89296.77
06:26:47
```

(Compose's container start-up lines trimmed.) Both containers print the same boot id: one kernel, so one `CLOCK_REALTIME`. `date -s` parses the date and is refused, because an ordinary container lacks the capability to set the clock; even a privileged one could only set it for every container on the host at once. Inside the new time namespace the uptime jumps by exactly 86,400 seconds while the wall clock reads the same second. Your boot id, uptime and wall-clock time will differ.

sections.h: Last write wins drops the write that came second
sections.body:
Many databases settle two writes to the same key by timestamp: keep the one with the highest, drop the other. That rule is **last write wins** (LWW). The Replication track's lesson on concurrent writes met it next to version vectors; this lesson asks where the timestamps come from. Cassandra and ScyllaDB take them from the client: the Java driver stamps each statement with the client machine's clock in microseconds, so a replica never has to ask anyone what time it is.

Here is what that does to a payment, step by step in the stepper. Pod A writes `captured`, stamped 10:00:00.002 by its clock. Pod B, whose clock is 15 ms behind, reads `captured` 6 ms later and writes `refunded`. B's stamp says 09:59:59.993, so the replica keeps `captured`, drops `refunded`, and says OK to both. Nothing logs an error. The refund was acknowledged and is gone, and B keeps losing: every B write that follows an A write is dropped until B's clock passes the highest stamp A wrote.

The skew doesn't need to be large. It only has to be larger than the gap between two **causally related** writes, where the second was decided after its writer saw the first. In the lab the gap is 6 ms: a skew of 6 ms loses nothing, 7 ms loses every write from the slow pod that follows one from the fast pod. With 0 to 50 ms of think time between writes, a 10 ms skew loses 4% of acknowledged writes, 20 ms loses 14%, and 100 ms or more loses half, every write the slow pod makes. Over the public internet, NTP errors of 10 to 20 ms are ordinary.

Kyle Kingsbury measured this in Cassandra in 2013. His clients updated one cell at QUORUM, one at a time, behind a perfect external lock, and Cassandra still lost 285 of 1,009 acknowledged writes, about 28%: the timestamps, not the lock's order, decided which write survived.

Better NTP shrinks the window; it doesn't close it. The fixes stop comparing timestamps from different machines. Write immutable rows under unique keys (one row per status change, keyed by a UUID) and read them all. Use types that merge, such as Cassandra's sets and counters. Use a conditional write, the Paxos-based lightweight transaction from the Transactions track's NoSQL lesson. Or make the order explicit with version vectors (the Replication track) or a logical clock, lesson 6 of this track. When you do need real time, the next section shows how to get it safely.

stepper.title: Last write wins with one slow clock
stepper.intro: The trace from the lab's `LwwDemo`: one register 1 ms away, pod-b's clock 15 ms behind. Stamps show the seconds and milliseconds after 10:00 (or before it).

frames.say: Four writes, four OKs, and the refund and the chargeback are gone. No log line, no exception. The skew only had to be larger than the 6 ms between a write and the next causally later one. The lab's `LwwDemo` printed this exact trace.

try.title: How much skew loses how much
steps: Predict: two pods take turns updating one status, each reading it first, with 0 to 50 ms of think time between writes. What share of acknowledged writes is lost with 20 ms of skew? With 1 second?
Run the demo. It prints the stepper's trace, then 1,000 writes for each skew.
Why does the loss stop growing at 50%? Rerun the trace part with `-Pargs='5'`.
try.expect:
```text
pod-b's clock is 15 ms behind. Each write follows a read of the one before it.
round  writer  value       true time      stamp          after the OK, a read returns
1      pod-a   captured    10:00:00.002   10:00:00.002   captured
2      pod-b   refunded    10:00:00.008   09:59:59.993   captured   <- lost
3      pod-a   settled     10:00:00.014   10:00:00.014   settled
4      pod-b   chargeback  10:00:00.020   10:00:00.005   settled   <- lost

1,000 writes alternating between the pods, 0 to 50 ms of think time between them
pod-b behind   acknowledged     lost
0 ms                   1000     0.0%
5 ms                   1000     0.0%
10 ms                  1000     4.2%
20 ms                  1000    13.8%
50 ms                  1000    42.8%
100 ms                 1000    50.0%
1000 ms                1000    50.0%
```

Every write is acknowledged. Losses start once the skew is larger than some of the gaps between a fast-pod write and the next slow-pod write (6 ms plus think time), and stop at 50%: once the skew is larger than every gap, each slow-pod write is lost and each fast-pod write survives. With `-Pargs='5'` the trace loses nothing: 5 ms is less than the 6 ms gap.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra Java driver: query timestamps

sections.h: Clocks that admit their error: TrueTime, ClockBound and commit wait
sections.body:
The fixes above give up on wall-clock order. Sometimes you need it: a transaction that starts after another has committed must see its writes, even when the two run on machines that never talk. Google's Spanner gets that from a clock that admits its error.

TrueTime's `now()` doesn't return a time. It returns an interval, earliest to latest, that contains the true time as long as the clock hardware stays within its assumptions. Google keeps the interval small with GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacenter. The 2012 Spanner paper gives its half-width, ε, as a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms over each 30-second poll, 4 ms most of the time, with 200 ppm of assumed drift: the shape in section 2's figure.

Spanner's commit uses the interval twice. It stamps a transaction with a time no earlier than `latest`, so the stamp is not yet in the past on any honest clock. Then, before it lets anyone see the commit, it waits until `earliest` has passed the stamp: now the stamp is in the past on every honest clock. This is **commit wait**, and it lasts about 2ε. Any transaction that starts after that moment, on any machine, reads a `latest` later than the stamp and gets a larger one. Timestamp order now matches real-time order, with no message between the two machines. The lab builds exactly this, and the Try shows the price: the wait is about twice the bound.

So ε is the number that matters. With TrueTime's 2012 figures it costs several milliseconds per commit. With AWS's 2023 bounds under 40 µs, it would be under 100 µs, and ClockBound hands the interval to any program; YugabyteDB can use ClockBound as its time source on AWS. CockroachDB takes another road. It doesn't wait on every commit: it assumes a maximum offset between nodes, 500 ms by default and 250 ms recommended for new multi-region clusters. A read that finds a value stamped a little above its own read time, within that offset, can't tell whether the value was written before it started, so it restarts at a later time.

Both designs are only as good as the bound, and both check it. A CockroachDB node shuts itself down when its clock is out of sync with at least half of the other nodes by 80% of the maximum offset; YugabyteDB servers stop when the skew passes their own 500 ms limit. The lab's last test shows why: a pod that is 20 ms behind but believes its bound is 5 ms loses writes even with commit wait. The Consistency and consensus track's lesson on distributed SQL builds on this, and lesson 6 of this track orders events with no physical clock at all.

try.title: The price of commit wait
steps: The same causal chain as before, but each pod stamps with `latest` and waits until `earliest` passes the stamp. Both pods sync every second. Predict pod-b's average wait when its clock is 20 ms behind and its bound is an honest 20 ms.
Run the demo. The last row lies: pod-b is 20 ms behind but claims a 5 ms bound.
Why does pod-a wait 3 ms even though its clock is exact?
try.expect:
```text
pod-b's clock                          lost  pod-a waits (avg)  pod-b waits (avg)
1 ms behind, bound 1 ms                   0             3.0 ms             3.0 ms
4 ms behind, bound 4 ms                   0             3.0 ms             9.0 ms
7 ms behind, bound 7 ms                   0             3.0 ms            15.0 ms
20 ms behind, bound 20 ms                 0             3.0 ms            41.0 ms
250 ms behind, bound 250 ms               0             3.0 ms           501.0 ms
20 ms behind, bound claims 5 ms          71             3.0 ms            11.0 ms
```

With honest bounds nothing is lost, even 250 ms behind, and the price is the wait: about twice the bound (each bound is the stated one plus about 1 ms of assumed drift since the last sync, and the wait starts after the store's 2 ms round trip). pod-a's clock is exact but it can't know that, so it waits out its own 1 ms bound plus drift too. With a bound that lies, commit wait is not long enough and 71 of 1,000 acknowledged writes are lost.

refs.title: Corbett et al.: Spanner, Google's globally distributed database (OSDI 2012)

analogy: Two tills in one shop print the time on every receipt, and till B runs 15 seconds slow. A customer buys a jacket at till A and returns it at till B ten seconds later. Sort the receipts by printed time and the return comes before the purchase, so the books say the jacket was never returned. Commit wait is a shop rule: each till knows it may be up to 15 seconds off, prints the latest time it could be, and holds the receipt until 30 seconds have passed, so any later receipt anywhere must print a later time. The analogy breaks on the numbers and on who watches: tills are off by seconds and a clerk would notice, while servers are off by milliseconds, write thousands of times a second, and no person ever reads the stamps.
in_your_world: Look for every place two machines' clocks are compared. An Oracle `created_at` filled with `SYSTIMESTAMP` comes from one database server's clock, so rows in one database are ordered consistently; a `created_at` set by each Quarkus pod with `Instant.now()` is not, and sorting a ledger by it can put a refund before its capture. Kafka records carry the producer's clock by default (`message.timestamp.type=CreateTime`), so windows over event time inherit every producer's skew, which the Stream processing track deals with. Inside Temporal workflow code, `Workflow.currentTimeMillis()` is the only clock you may read, because it comes from the workflow's history and replays identically. For your own timeouts and retry budgets, use `System.nanoTime()` or `TimeSource.Monotonic`. And make services take a `java.time.Clock` (a CDI producer in Quarkus) instead of calling `Instant.now()`: that is the only way to test them with a skewed or jumping clock, since a container can't have its own wall clock.
mistake: The common mistake is measuring durations with the wall clock: `val start = System.currentTimeMillis()`, then `if (System.currentTimeMillis() - start > timeoutMs)`, or latency metrics computed from two `Instant.now()` calls. It works in every test, because test machines rarely step their clocks, so it ships. Then NTP steps a pod's clock back after a long period without sync, or forward after a VM migration, and timeouts fire at once or never, retry budgets go negative, and a percentile panel shows negative latencies. The fix is mechanical: `System.nanoTime()` or `TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow()` for every duration and deadline, compared as `System.nanoTime() - start >= timeoutNanos` (subtract first; the JDK warns that comparing two `nanoTime` values directly breaks when the counter wraps). Keep the wall clock for timestamps people or other machines will read.

compare.title: Timing an issuer call

a.label: Wall clock: wrong across a step
a.title: IssuerTimer.kt
a.src:
val start = System.currentTimeMillis()
val code = issuer.authorize(key, amount)
val tookMs = System.currentTimeMillis() - start        // an NTP step in between: wrong, maybe negative
latency.record(tookMs)

b.label: Monotonic clock: always a duration
b.title: IssuerTimer.kt
b.src:
val mark = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow()             // reads System.nanoTime() on the JVM
val code = issuer.authorize(key, amount)
val took = mark.elapsedNow()                          // a Duration, never negative
latency.record(took.inWholeMilliseconds)

compare.note: Both read a clock twice and subtract. The left one reads `CLOCK_REALTIME`, which NTP, an operator or a leap second can move in either direction between the two reads. The right one reads `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` through Kotlin's `TimeSource.Monotonic`, which only ever moves forward, so `elapsedNow()` is a real duration. The wall clock's number is still the right thing to log next to the result, as the moment the call happened.

worked.title: Commit wait, built from a clock that admits its error

steps.say: Model a node's clock in virtual time: the true time, plus the offset it had at its last sync, plus the drift since. The node can read this number but not the offset inside it.
What the node does know is a bound: how far off it was allowed to be at the sync, plus the worst drift it assumes since. Round up; a bound must never undershoot.
Report the reading the way TrueTime and ClockBound do, as an interval that holds the true time if the bound is honest.
steps.code:
fun bounds(): TimeInterval = millis().let { now ->
    val e = errorBoundMs()
    TimeInterval(now - e, now + e)
}

steps.say: Stamp a write with `latest`: the true time can't be later than that yet, so no write that already happened anywhere can carry a larger stamp from an honest clock.
steps.code:
val stamp = clock.bounds().latest
store.write(Write(value, stamp, name)) { /* acknowledged */ }

steps.say: Wait until `earliest` passes the stamp before telling anyone the write is done. From then on every honest clock reads later than the stamp, so every causally later write gets a larger one. The wait is about 2ε.

lab.title: Drifting clocks, a register that loses writes, and commit wait
steps: Read the given parts: `Sim` keeps the true time (it starts at 10:00:00 UTC on 7 November 2026), `DriftingClock` is a `java.time.Clock` so code can take it wherever it takes `Clock.systemUTC()`, and `causalChain` in `Registers.kt` runs writers that each read the register before writing. Run the tests from the `labs` folder: all 16 fail.

Exercise 1: `DriftingClock.millis`, `errorBoundMs` and `bounds`. Run `--tests 'sfz.dist.l03.ClockTest'`: 8 pass, including 17.28 s a day at 200 ppm, the 1-to-7 ms sawtooth, a sync that moves the clock backward, and a jqwik property that an honest interval always contains the true time.
Exercise 2: `LwwRegister.apply`. The tests with plain writes now pass, among them `a writer whose clock is 20 ms behind loses every write that follows the other's`: 100 OKs, 50 writes gone.

Exercise 3: `Writer.writeWithCommitWait`. Run all 16. The property test tries 200 random offsets, bounds, think times and seeds and finds no lost write; `commit wait is only as good as the bound` finds some.
hints: `millis`: `sim.now + offsetAtSync + (sim.now - syncedAt) * driftPpm / 1_000_000`. Long division, so 0.5 ms of drift reads as 0.
`errorBoundMs`: `Math.ceilDiv(a, b)` rounds a positive division up (JDK 18+, and the labs compile for 21).
LWW tie-break: `write.timestampMs == c.timestampMs && write.writer > c.writer`. Compare strings with `>`; Kotlin uses `compareTo`.

In `writeWithCommitWait`, read `clock.bounds().latest` once, before sending. Inside the store's ack, define a local `fun check()` that calls `done` or reschedules itself with `sim.after(1) { check() }`.

drill.title: Commit wait from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `writeWithCommitWait(value, done)` given `clock.bounds()`, `store.write(write, ack)` and `sim.after(ms, action)`. Then answer in one comment each: why is the stamp `latest` and not the plain reading, and why does the wait end when `earliest` passes the stamp?

recap: Wall clocks (`currentTimeMillis`, `CLOCK_REALTIME`) give points in time and can jump either way; monotonic clocks (`nanoTime`, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) give durations and mean nothing across machines.
Quartz drifts up to about 200 ppm, 17 s a day; NTP over the internet keeps clocks within tens of ms, and hardware timestamps and PTP bring cloud bounds under 100 µs (AWS: under 40 µs).
Containers share the host's wall clock; time namespaces offset only monotonic and boot clocks, so skew goes into tests through `java.time.Clock`.

Last write wins with client timestamps silently drops a causally later write whenever the writer's clock lags by more than the gap between the writes; Jepsen lost 28% of acknowledged Cassandra writes.
A clock that reports [earliest, latest] lets Spanner commit-wait about 2ε so timestamp order matches real-time order; CockroachDB instead assumes a max offset (500 ms) and restarts uncertain reads.
Every such design depends on the bound being true, so nodes that drift past it shut themselves down.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: a heartbeat monitor computes silence as `System.currentTimeMillis() - lastSeen` for each node. NTP steps the monitor's own clock forward by 3 seconds. What happens?
options: Nothing: every node's silence grows by the same amount, so the comparison is fair
Every node looks 3 seconds quieter at once, and a monitor with a timeout under that suspects the whole cluster
The monitor's phi values drop, so it becomes more patient
The nodes' heartbeats carry their own timestamps, so the step cancels out
quiz.why: The silence is computed from the monitor's wall clock, which just jumped 3 seconds, so every node's silence jumped too. A detector with a timeout under 3 seconds suspects everyone at once, the cascade lesson 2 warned about. Measuring silence with `nanoTime()` makes the step invisible. That everyone is affected equally is exactly the problem: the detector's input is wrong for all of them.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct use of `System.nanoTime()`?
options: Stamping a ledger row so another service can order it against its own rows
Checking whether a 2-second deadline for an issuer call has passed, within one JVM
Comparing when two pods received the same Kafka record
Storing a payment's creation time in Oracle
quiz.why: `nanoTime` measures elapsed time within one JVM, which is exactly a deadline. Its origin is arbitrary and differs between JVMs, so its values mean nothing to another service, another pod or a database row. Those need a wall-clock timestamp, with its error in mind.

quiz.q: Two servers both sync with NTP every 64 seconds. One oscillator runs 150 ppm fast, the other 120 ppm slow. Ignoring NTP's own error, about how far apart can their clocks get just before a sync?
options: About 1.6 µs
About 17 ms
About 1.7 s
About 23 s
quiz.why: In 64 seconds the fast clock gains 64 × 150 µs = 9.6 ms and the slow one loses 64 × 120 µs = 7.7 ms, so they can be about 17 ms apart; the lab's `DriftDemo` measured 16 ms. 23 s is the skew after a whole day with no sync at all. In practice NTP's own error, tens of milliseconds over the internet, comes on top.

quiz.q: Pod B's clock is 30 ms behind pod A's. Using Cassandra's client-side timestamps, B updates a payment's status 200 ms after A did, with nothing reading in between. Is B's write lost?
options: Yes: B's clock is behind, so its writes always lose
No: 200 ms later in real time is still 170 ms later by B's clock, so B's stamp is higher
Yes: concurrent writes in Cassandra are always resolved in favour of the first
It depends on which replica the coordinator picks
quiz.why: LWW loses a write only when the clock skew is larger than the real-time gap between the two writes. 200 − 30 leaves B's stamp 170 ms above A's. The danger zone is the causal chain where writes follow each other closely: a refund decided 6 ms after the capture, with 15 ms of skew, is lost.

quiz.q: A database uses commit wait with a clock whose bound is ε = 4 ms. An operator turns off the time daemon on one node, and its bound keeps assuming 200 ppm while its real drift is 900 ppm. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: commit wait makes ordering independent of clock accuracy
Commit waits get longer but remain correct
Once the real error exceeds the assumed bound, a node can stamp a causally later write below an earlier one, and ordering breaks silently
The database refuses all writes immediately
quiz.why: Commit wait is correct only if the true time really lies inside [earliest, latest]. A node whose drift is worse than assumed reports a bound that lies, so its waits are too short and its stamps can fall below earlier ones, the lab's lying-bound test. That is why CockroachDB and YugabyteDB shut down nodes whose clocks leave the allowed offset, and why TrueTime assumes a conservative drift.

flashcards.front: Wall clock or monotonic clock for a timeout?
flashcards.back: Monotonic: `System.nanoTime()` or `TimeSource.Monotonic`. The wall clock can be stepped backward or forward between two reads.
An NTP step, an operator setting the clock, a leap second inserted by stepping back, or a VM resuming after a pause or migration.

flashcards.front: What does 200 ppm of drift mean per day?
flashcards.back: 200 µs per second, so 17.28 seconds a day for a clock nobody corrects.

flashcards.front: Why can't you give one Docker container a skewed wall clock?
flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel's `CLOCK_REALTIME`. Time namespaces offset only monotonic and boot clocks. Inject skew through a `java.time.Clock` instead.

flashcards.front: When does last write wins lose a causally later write?
flashcards.back: When the later writer's clock lags the earlier writer's by more than the real time between the two writes. The store drops it and still says OK.
Stamp a commit with the clock's `latest`, then wait until `earliest` passes the stamp before acknowledging. About 2ε; afterwards every later commit anywhere gets a larger stamp.
A maximum offset (500 ms default): reads restart when they meet values in their uncertainty window, and a node out of sync with half the cluster by 80% of the max offset shuts down.

terms.plain: The wall clock: the current date and time, kept close to UTC by corrections that can jump it.
A counter that only moves forward, for measuring durations on one machine.
How much faster or slower a clock runs than true time, in parts per million.
Correcting a clock by running it slightly fast or slow for a while instead of jumping it.
Resolving conflicting writes by keeping the one with the highest timestamp and dropping the rest.
How far the node's clock may be from true time; TrueTime and ClockBound return it as [earliest, latest].
Waiting until the clock's earliest possible time passes a commit's stamp before acknowledging it.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague proposes ordering payment events from three services by their `Instant.now()` timestamps, "since all our pods run NTP". Explain what can go wrong, with numbers, and what you'd do instead.
explain_back.answer: NTP keeps each pod near UTC, but not exactly: over a normal network the error is milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, a step can move a clock by hundreds of milliseconds, and a VM migration can jump it seconds. So two pods' clocks can disagree by more than the time between two related events. If the refund service writes a refund 6 ms after the capture service wrote the capture, and the refund pod's clock is 15 ms behind, the refund gets the earlier timestamp. Sorting by time puts it before the capture, and a last-write-wins store keeps the capture and silently drops the refund, while saying OK to both. Better NTP only shrinks that window. Instead I'd avoid comparing clocks from different machines: give each payment one place that orders its events (a database sequence, or a per-payment version checked with a conditional write), or keep the events as immutable rows and merge them, or carry a logical clock. If we truly need real-time order across machines, we need a clock that reports its error, like ClockBound, and to wait out that error before acknowledging, which is what Spanner does.

deeper.body:
**How NTP estimates the offset.** With t1 the client's send time, t2 the server's receive time, t3 the server's send time and t4 the client's receive time, the offset estimate is ((t2 − t1) + (t3 − t4)) / 2 and the round trip is (t4 − t1) − (t3 − t2). The estimate is exact only if both directions took the same time; any asymmetry ends up, halved, in the offset. chrony and ntpd combine many samples from several servers and discard outliers, and both report a root dispersion and root delay, which is where ClockBound's bound starts: the absolute offset, plus the root dispersion, plus half the root delay.

**Leap smearing.** Google's public NTP servers spread a leap second over 24 hours, noon to noon UTC, by slowing their clocks by about 11.6 ppm, well inside what NTP clients can follow. AWS's NTP endpoint is smeared too, while its PTP hardware clock is not, so AWS advises against mixing the two sources on one host. With leap seconds reportedly ending in 2027, smearing becomes history. The bigger fear had been the first negative leap second ever, a day one second short, which almost no software has been tested against.

**Hybrid logical clocks** keep a 64-bit timestamp close to physical time while guaranteeing that a message's receiver stamps later than its sender, whatever the clocks say. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use them alongside their offset limits. Lesson 6 builds one.

*Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 9, covers clocks and the trouble with relying on them in the same order; note that its leap-second date predates the reported 2026 decision.
